overview.text: Keratin is a group of fibrous structural proteins found in vertebrates, built from amino-acid chains that assemble into strong fibers. It matters because it reinforces and protects the epidermis and forms many structures made from skin, including human hair and nails and, in other animals, feathers, beaks, claws, horns, hooves, and scales. In skin, keratin-packed outer cells create a tough surface barrier; they are shed and replaced by cells from below. Keratins differ in structure: α-keratin chains coil into helices, while β-keratin has a pleated-sheet-like backbone. Chemical cross-links help stabilize keratin’s structure and make it resistant to ordinary physical and chemical damage.

key_facts.text: Keratin proteins are made from amino-acid building blocks linked into chains.
Cross-links between keratin chains help stabilize the structure and make it resistant to ordinary damage.
Keratin makes the epidermis’s outer surface mechanically tough; shedding those cells also removes microbes clinging to the surface.
α-keratin has a coiled-coil, alpha-helical structure; β-keratin has a zigzag or pleated-sheet-like structure.
Hair, nails, feathers, beaks, claws, horns, hooves, and scales are examples of specialized keratin-containing structures.
